blocks.text: 1. Introduction

You just learned how to load data into a DataFrame, from a CSV, a spreadsheet, a database query, wherever it came from. Now that DataFrame is sitting in memory, and you have absolutely no idea what is actually in it. Is it 50 rows or 5 million? Does every column hold the type of value you expect? Are there gaps where data should be but is not? You do not find any of that out by staring at the variable name. You find it out by running a small, repeatable routine of inspection commands, every single time, before you write a single line of analysis.

This lesson is that routine. Think of it as the equivalent of glancing at the dashboard before you drive a car you just rented. You do not need to understand every wire under the hood, but you do want to know the fuel gauge is not sitting on empty before you pull onto the highway. Pandas gives you a handful of methods, mostly one line each, that together tell you the shape of your data, what is inside it, and where it might already be broken.

blocks.alt: A fresh DataFrame branching out to head and tail, shape, info, describe, and dtypes
blocks.caption: The first look toolkit: five quick checks before you do anything else.

blocks.text: None of these methods change your data. They only look at it and report back. That makes them completely safe to run as many times as you want, on any DataFrame, at any point. Get comfortable running all of them out of habit, the same way you would check your mirrors before changing lanes.
2. Peeking at Your Data with head and tail

The very first thing to do with any new DataFrame is look at it. Not the whole thing, just a slice. df.head() shows you the first five rows by default, and df.tail() shows you the last five. Pass a number in if you want more or fewer, like df.head(10).

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

df.head()   # first 5 rows
df.tail(3)  # last 3 rows

blocks.alt: A DataFrame branching into head returning the first five rows and tail returning the last five rows
blocks.caption: head shows you the top of the table, tail shows you the bottom.

blocks.text: Why bother with both ends instead of just the top? Because a lot of real problems only show up at the boundaries. A file that was supposed to have clean daily records for a full year might have its last few rows cut off mid write, or padded with a trailing summary row that is not actual data at all. Looking only at the top would never catch that.

items: head confirms the columns loaded with the names and order you expected.
head lets you eyeball whether values look reasonable, like ages that are actually between 0 and 120.
tail catches broken or incomplete rows near the end of a file.
tail is useful for time series data, where the last rows are usually the most recent and most relevant.

blocks.title: A habit worth building
blocks.content: Run head right after every read_csv, read_excel, or database query, before you do anything else. It takes one second and it catches an enormous number of silly mistakes early, like loading the wrong file or a delimiter that split columns incorrectly.

blocks.text: 3. Shape: How Many Rows and Columns

If you have worked through the NumPy material already, .shape should feel familiar. On a DataFrame it works the same way it does on an array: it returns a tuple of two numbers, the row count first and the column count second.

blocks.alt: A DataFrame pointing to its shape attribute, which splits into row count and column count
blocks.caption: shape hands you two numbers, rows then columns, in a single glance.

blocks.text: This one number pair answers a surprising number of questions instantly. Did the join you just ran actually add rows, or did it silently drop half of them? Does this dataset even have enough rows to be useful for training a model? Did a filter you applied earlier remove more than you meant it to? Checking shape before and after any operation that reshapes your data is one of the cheapest sanity checks you can run.

items: df.shape[0] gives you just the row count.
df.shape[1] gives you just the column count.
len(df) is a shorter way to get the row count on its own.

blocks.text: 4. Info: The Dense Summary

head shows you a slice, shape shows you a size. df.info() shows you the structure. It is the single most information dense command in this entire lesson, printing every column name, how many non null values it has, and its dtype, all in one shot.

code.content:
df.info()

# <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
# RangeIndex: 1000 entries, 0 to 999
# Data columns (total 5 columns):
#  #   Column         Non-Null Count  Dtype
# ---  ------         --------------  -----
#  0   customer_id    1000 non-null   int64
#  1   signup_date    1000 non-null   object
#  2   phone_number   812 non-null    object
#  3   plan_type      1000 non-null   object
#  4   monthly_spend  1000 non-null   float64
# dtypes: float64(1), int64(1), object(3)
# memory usage: 39.2+ KB

blocks.alt: A DataFrame branching into info, which lists column names, non null counts, and dtypes
blocks.caption: info gives you names, non null counts, and dtypes together, in one call.

blocks.text: Read that output like a table with three columns of its own: the column name, how many non null entries it has out of the total row count, and what type pandas decided the column is. That middle number is doing more work than it looks like it is.
4.1 Spotting Missing Values Early

Look again at the sample output above. The DataFrame has 1000 rows total, and most columns say 1000 non null. But phone_number says 812 non null. That gap, 188 rows, is 188 missing phone numbers you did not know about a second ago.

blocks.alt: The info non null count column showing signup_date fully populated at 1000 non null while phone_number is short at 812 non null, revealing 188 missing values
blocks.caption: A shorter non null count than the total row count is usually the first sign of missing data.

blocks.text: This is genuinely one of the most common ways people first discover that a dataset has missing values. Not from a warning message, not from a crash, just from a number in an info summary that does not match the row count. Catching it here, right at the start, means you get to decide what to do about it deliberately, instead of finding out three steps later when a calculation silently ignores those rows or a model training step throws an error.

blocks.title: This gets its own lesson later
blocks.content: Deciding what to actually do about missing values, drop the rows, fill them with a default, fill them with a computed value, is a bigger topic with real tradeoffs. This lesson is only about noticing they exist. The dedicated missing values lesson covers the fixes.

blocks.text: 5. Describe: Summary Statistics

info tells you the shape of your columns. df.describe() tells you the shape of the numbers inside them. Run it on a DataFrame and, by default, it summarizes every numeric column with count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, the three quartiles, and maximum.

blocks.alt: describe producing count, mean, standard deviation, min, quartiles, and max for numeric columns
blocks.caption: describe compresses an entire numeric column into eight summary numbers.

blocks.text: Skim these numbers before you trust anything else you do with the data. A max monthly_spend of 220 next to a mean of 42 is worth a second look, is that a real high value customer, or a data entry error where someone typed an extra digit? A min of 0 might be perfectly normal, or it might mean some rows were never actually charged. describe will not answer those questions for you, but it puts them in front of you immediately.

items: count tells you how many non null values went into the statistics, a second way to catch missing data.
mean and std describe the center and spread of the column.
min and max are your fastest way to catch outliers and obviously wrong values.
the 25%, 50%, and 75% rows are the quartiles, with 50% being the median.

blocks.text: 5.1 Describing Non-Numeric Columns with include=all

By default describe quietly skips any column that is not numeric, text columns, category columns, all of it gets left out. Pass include="all" and it summarizes every column instead, numeric and non numeric together, filling in whichever statistics make sense for each type.

code.content:
df.describe(include="all")

#        customer_id signup_date phone_number plan_type  monthly_spend
# count   1000.000000        1000          812      1000    1000.000000
# unique          NaN         365          801         3            NaN
# top             NaN  2025-01-14   9876543210     basic            NaN
# freq            NaN           7            2       540            NaN
# mean     500.500000         NaN          NaN       NaN      42.318000
# ...

blocks.alt: describe with include equals all splitting into numeric columns getting the usual stats and text columns getting unique, top, and freq
blocks.caption: include=all adds unique, top, and freq for text and object columns.

blocks.text: For a non numeric column, you get unique, which is how many distinct values show up, top, which is the most frequent value, and freq, which is how many times that top value appears. Notice plan_type has only 3 unique values and basic shows up 540 times out of 1000 rows, that alone tells you a lot about how customers are distributed across plans, before you have written a single groupby.
6. Dtypes: A Focused Look at Column Types

info gives you dtypes as one column among several. Sometimes you just want that column, on its own, without everything else. df.dtypes gives you exactly that, a clean list of every column name next to its type.

code.content:
df.dtypes

# customer_id        int64
# signup_date       object
# phone_number      object
# plan_type         object
# monthly_spend    float64
# dtype: object

blocks.alt: A DataFrame with age typed as int64, price typed as float64, and category typed as object
blocks.caption: dtypes lists every column next to the type pandas actually assigned it.

blocks.text: int64 and float64 are what you would expect for whole numbers and decimals. object is the odd one out, it is the catch all type pandas uses for text, and also for any column that mixes types or that pandas simply could not confidently parse as a number.
6.1 When a Numeric Column Turns Into an Object

Here is a gotcha you will run into constantly with real world data. You load a file, you check dtypes, and a column you were completely sure should be numeric, price, quantity, score, whatever it is, comes back as object instead of int64 or float64.

blocks.alt: A price column that was expected to be float64 but is actually object dtype because a stray piece of text is hiding somewhere inside it
blocks.caption: An unexpectedly object typed numeric column almost always means a stray non numeric value is hiding in there.

blocks.text: Almost every time, the cause is the same: somewhere in that column, buried among thousands of clean numbers, there is at least one value that is not actually a number. Maybe someone typed "unknown" instead of leaving a cell blank. Maybe a currency symbol snuck into one row. Maybe a stray space or a typo like "1O" with a letter O instead of a zero got entered by hand. Pandas cannot call the whole column numeric if even one entry does not fit, so it falls back to object and treats every value, including the real numbers, as text.

blocks.title: Why this matters beyond just labeling
blocks.content: An object typed numeric column will silently break math. Sorting behaves like string sorting instead of numeric sorting, and any arithmetic you try to run on it will raise an error the moment it hits that one bad value. Catching this at the dtypes check, before you try to compute anything, saves you from a confusing error message later.

blocks.text: The fix itself belongs to a later lesson on cleaning and type conversion, but the discovery step belongs here. The moment dtypes surprises you, you already know exactly where to go looking.
7. Columns and Index: The Axis Labels
A DataFrame has two sets of labels, one for each side. df.columns gives you the labels running across the top, the column names. df.index gives you the labels running down the side, one per row.

code.content:
df.columns
# Index(['customer_id', 'signup_date', 'phone_number', 'plan_type', 'monthly_spend'], dtype='object')

df.index
# RangeIndex(start=0, stop=1000, step=1)

blocks.alt: A DataFrame branching into columns for the labels across the top and index for the labels down the side
blocks.caption: columns and index are the two label axes that frame every DataFrame.

blocks.text: Most of the time index is just a plain range of numbers starting at 0, like the example above, which is what pandas assigns automatically if you never told it otherwise. But it does not have to be. Dates, customer IDs, or any column you choose can become the index instead, and when that happens, checking df.index right away tells you whether that setup actually happened the way you expected.

items: df.columns.tolist() turns the column labels into a plain Python list, handy for looping or checking membership.
A quick "expected_col" in df.columns check catches typos before they turn into a KeyError three lines later.
df.index is worth checking after any merge, groupby, or reset_index call, since all three can change it in ways you did not intend.

blocks.text: 8. Checking for Duplicate Rows

One more quick check belongs in this first pass: are there rows that are exact copies of each other? df.duplicated() returns a True or False for every row, True meaning that row is a repeat of an earlier one.

code.content:
df.duplicated().sum()
# 14   meaning 14 rows are exact duplicates of an earlier row

blocks.alt: DataFrame rows running through duplicated, which flags repeat rows True and sum totals how many duplicates exist
blocks.caption: duplicated flags repeat rows, and summing it gives you a quick duplicate count.

blocks.text: You do not need to act on this right now, and you definitely do not need to decide the right way to remove duplicates in this lesson. All you are doing here is noticing. A count of 14 duplicate rows out of 1000 is a fact worth knowing the moment you load the data, even if the actual cleanup happens later.

blocks.title: Coming up in a later lesson
blocks.content: Dropping duplicates properly, deciding which copy to keep, and deciding what counts as a duplicate in the first place, like matching on some columns but not others, gets its own dedicated lesson. For now, duplicated and sum are just one more line in your first look routine.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: A First Look at a Messy DataFrame
Let us put the whole routine together on one dataset, the way you actually would the moment a new file lands on your desk. Say you just loaded a small file of product listings.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
df.head()

#    product_id   name        price  in_stock
# 0           1  Mug          9.99      True
# 1           2  Notebook     4.50      True
# 2           3  Backpack    "N/A"     False
# 3           4  Water Bottle 12.00      True
# 4           5  Pen           1.25      True

blocks.text: Already, head is doing its job. Row 2 has a price of "N/A" sitting inside quotes, which looks suspicious in a column that should otherwise be plain decimal numbers. Keep going with the routine instead of jumping to conclusions yet.

code.content:
df.shape
# (250, 4)

df.info()

# <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'>
# RangeIndex: 250 entries, 0 to 249
# Data columns (total 4 columns):
#  #   Column      Non-Null Count  Dtype
# ---  ------      --------------  -----
#  0   product_id  250 non-null    int64
#  1   name        250 non-null    object
#  2   price       250 non-null    object
#  3   in_stock    250 non-null    bool
# dtypes: bool(1), int64(1), object(2)
# memory usage: 6.2 KB

blocks.text: shape confirms 250 rows and 4 columns, matching what you expected from the file. But info raises a flag right away: price shows up as object, not float64. Every non null count reads 250, so nothing is missing here, this is purely a typing problem, not a missing data problem.

code.content:
df.dtypes

# product_id     int64
# name          object
# price         object
# in_stock        bool
# dtype: object

blocks.text: dtypes confirms it a second way: price is object. Given what head already showed you, the "N/A" text sitting in row 2 is almost certainly the reason. One stray non numeric value was enough to push the entire column out of float64 and into object.

code.content:
df[df["price"].apply(lambda v: not str(v).replace(".", "", 1).isdigit())]

#    product_id      name  price  in_stock
# 2           3  Backpack    N/A     False

blocks.text: That last line filters the column down to whatever does not look like a plain number, and there it is: row 2, the Backpack, with price stored as the text "N/A" instead of an actual missing value or a number. This is exactly the kind of thing describe would have made harder to spot, since describe by default silently skips object columns altogether.

Notice price is completely missing from that output, no mean, no max, nothing, because pandas cannot compute statistics on an object typed column. That absence is itself a clue pointing straight back to the dtypes problem you already found. Chase describe with include="all" instead and price would show up again, but only with unique, top, and freq, never with a mean.

blocks.alt: The full first look routine running from head and tail, into shape, into info, into describe, into dtypes
blocks.caption: The same five checks, run in order, catch nearly every early problem in a new dataset.

blocks.text: Five commands, run in the same order every time, just uncovered a real data quality issue before a single calculation was attempted. That is the entire point of this lesson. head and tail gave you a first look, shape confirmed the size, info flagged the object dtype, dtypes confirmed it, and a quick filter pinned down exactly which row was responsible. Fixing it, converting price back to numeric and deciding what "N/A" should actually become, is a job for a later lesson on cleaning and type conversion.
10. Wrap-Up
Every one of these methods is read only, quick to run, and safe to call as often as you like. Make running them a reflex, not a task you remember to do only after something breaks.

items: Always look, do not assume. A dataset never behaves exactly the way its filename or documentation promises.
A non null count lower than the row count in info is your earliest signal of missing data.
An object dtype on a column you expected to be numeric almost always means a stray non numeric value snuck in somewhere.
None of this fixes anything by itself. It only tells you where to look next.

blocks.text: With this routine in your hands, you will never again run an analysis on a DataFrame you have not actually looked at first. The next lesson picks up exactly where the missing phone numbers and the N/A price left off: what to actually do once you have found the problems.
